To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we used iPSCs from MDS patients to generate cerebral organoids, and that these organoids showed a cell migration defect, increased apoptosis, and prolonged mitosis of a progenitor cell subtype that is critical for human neotropical development.
we have developed a new human model of lissencephalies, and we have identified the cell type that causes the disease and the cellular mechanism that causes the disease.

we generated cerebral organoids from MDS and control iPSCs and found that the outer radial glia in MDS cerebral organoids are mitotically impaired, which may explain their lack of cortical expansion in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the cerebral cortex and its disorders.
the cellular pathogenesis of MDS, which is caused by a chromosomal deletion that leads to the loss of the LIS1 gene.
the pathogenesis of MDS, which is a severe neurological disorder that causes mental retardation and epilepsy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have developed a novel and important model system for studying the cellular pathogenesis of lissencephalies.
cerebral organoids derived from MDS iPSCs are an excellent model for studying MDS and other lissencephalies, which can be used to identify novel drug targets for the disease.
cerebral organoids derived form MDS-iPSCs show a cell migration defect, increased horizontal cell divisions and a mitotic defect of outer radial glia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how the Miller-Dieker lissencephalies can be modeled in vitro using cerebral organoids.

cerebral organoids derived from Miller-Dieker Syndrome (MDS)-iPSCs have an impaired neurogenesis and an increased apoptosis, which are rescued by a correction of the MDS causatic chromosomal deletion.
we have used cerebral organoids, which are 3D models of the human developing brain, to model the cellular pathogenesis of Miller-Dieker Syndrome, which is a severe form of human lissencephalies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cerebral organoids derived from human induced pluripotent stem (iPSC) cells can recapitulate many features of lissencephalies, including the cell migration defect and the severe apoptosis of the neuroepithelial progenitors, and that these organoids can be used to model the cellular features of lissencesphaly and to test therapeutic approaches.
cerebral organoids can be a powerful tool to study human neurodevelopmental diseases.
we can model a human brain disease using cerebral organoids.
